transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-12 14:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Sophia Reyes (VectraVision Head of ML), Daniel Kim (Platform Eng), Aisha Singh (CTO)
Shared artifacts: Deck: /shared/vectra-poc-deck.pdf, Benchmark runbook link: https://redwood.example.com/poc-bench-runbook, Example script: /shared/benchmarks/run_bench.sh
----
[00:00:05] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll keep this to about 45-ish minutes but have 52 on the calendar, great to meet you all. quick intros?
[00:00:18] Sophia Reyes: hi i'm sophia, head of ml at vectra, we run recommendation and real-time personalization, latency is like our top constraint.
[00:00:25] Daniel Kim: daniel here, platform eng, i'll be doing the integration and running bench infra.
[00:00:30] Aisha Singh: aisha, cto, focused on reliability and SLAs.
[00:00:35] Maya Chen: awesome. liam, quick intro?
[00:00:38] Liam Patel: liam, solutions eng, i'll own the benchmark setup and analysis.
[00:00:42] Maya Chen: cool. goal today is to align on success criteria for the poc — particularly latency/throughput SLOs, how we measure TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, and the measurement plan and timeline.
[00:00:55] Sophia Reyes: yes, we're trying to decide between hosted and dedicated, and we need to be clear on what we accept for first token and per-token costs. our production critical path is the recommendation rerank call, that's where 95% of traffic hits.
[00:01:10] Maya Chen: makes sense. can you share rough numbers for request size, seq lengths, and concurrency?
[00:01:18] Daniel Kim: typical prompt length is ~120 tokens, outputs are ~40 tokens on average. peak concurrency per region ~120 concurrent requests, sustained at 60. p95 latency target we'd like sub-120ms for first token ideally, p99 under 300ms but that's aggressive.
[00:01:35] Liam Patel: couple clarifications — when you say p95 first token 120ms is that cold start included or warm-only?
[00:01:42] Sophia Reyes: we care mostly about warm latency; cold starts handled by warm pools. we also have burst windows where concurrency can jump to 250 for a few mins.
[00:01:51] Maya Chen: okay warm path is what we'll measure. quick note on terminology: we'll use TTFT to mean Time-To-First-Token (time from request accepted to first byte/token emitted) and TPOT as Time-Per-Output-Token (avg token generation tail latency per token) — that helps separate model tokenizer and decoding overhead from startup/dispatch.
[00:02:10] Daniel Kim: sounds good. do you have recommended p95/p99 split for TPOT?
[00:02:15] Liam Patel: for models similar to what you described, typical TPOT p95 is ~8-12ms/token on modern quantized variants on A10/NVIDIA T4 class, p99 maybe 25-40ms/token depending on seq length and KV cache behavior. those numbers vary with batching and beam settings.
[00:02:31] Sophia Reyes: we do beam 1, greedy. so batching is gonna be important. our SLA requires 95th for user-visible actions under 200ms for the whole call — so roughly TTFT + (avg_output_tokens * TPOT_p95) must be <=200ms.
[00:02:48] Maya Chen: right, so we need to map their end-to-end SLO into TTFT and TPOT targets. given 40 output tokens and desired 200ms end-to-end p95, that implies TTFT + 40*TPOT_p95 <= 200ms. if TTFT is 80ms, TPOT_p95 must be <=3ms/token — that's tight and may require batching optimizations and heavier quantization.
[00:03:10] Aisha Singh: that math is helpful. we also have strict p99 for incident detection at 500ms. it's looser but still important.
[00:03:18] Liam Patel: note that TPOT can be reduced by larger batches — but batching increases TTFT for first token due to wait time. tradeoff between throughput and first token. smart routing and prefix caching can help if many requests share prefixes.
[00:03:33] Sophia Reyes: our workloads have lots of similar prefixes for personalization; maybe caching will help. do you have guidance on measurement to separate scheduling/wait time from pure model decode?
[00:03:45] Liam Patel: yes we'll instrument both at client side and with the server-side timing headers. measurement plan we propose: 1) baseline warm single-request TTFT (no batching), 2) TPOT microbench (generate N tokens single-thread loop to measure pure decode), 3) traffic-shaped runs with target concurrency and batching configs, 4) p95/p99 extraction and analysis. we'll provide the runbook and scripts.
[00:04:05] Daniel Kim: will the runbook show exactly how to launch with our VPC and dedicated pool?
[00:04:10] Maya Chen: yes — for private or dedicated we provide run instructions and spot checks for kernel selection and GPU metrics. note some transcriptions in our logs may call KV cache as K-V cash, haha.
[00:04:20] Sophia Reyes: (laughs) noted. for the POC success criteria we'd like: p95 end-to-end <=200ms for the rerank route under typical load, p99 end-to-end <=500ms, and TPOT_p95 <= 6ms/token as a practical internal target — does that sound achievable?
[00:04:35] Liam Patel: 6ms/token p95 is reasonable with quantized models on good GPUs if we can do batching of 4-8 and keep the TTFT under 100ms. if you can't batch due to strict TTFT, then you'd need faster hardware or model distillation.
[00:04:48] Aisha Singh: what about measuring tokenization overhead? we see spikes when tokenizers run in Python vs C++ tokenizers.
[00:04:55] Liam Patel: good call — the runbook will have a tokenization microbenchmark and recommend using the tokenizers lib in Rust/C bindings to reduce that overhead. we'll capture client-side timing for tokenization start/end.
[00:05:06] Sophia Reyes: timeline: we'd like to run a first baseline next week, and then a 1-week continuous run to collect p95/p99 under production-like traffic. is that feasible?
[00:05:14] Maya Chen: yes. plan: share scripts by Monday, you (customer) provide dataset and traffic pattern by Wednesday, we run baseline Thursday, then schedule the 7-day run starting Friday.
[00:05:25] Daniel Kim: can we run the benchmark in our VPC with private deployment? we need KMS integration and audit logs.
[00:05:31] Maya Chen: absolutely, Private deployment supports KMS/HSM and audit logging. for the POC we can run on Dedicated or Private depending on your preference; dedicated is quicker to provision and we can mirror the same config later in Private.
[00:05:42] Sophia Reyes: provisioning times?
[00:05:44] Liam Patel: Dedicated pools typically provision in 24-48 hours; Private has more setup (networking/KMS) and can take a week+ depending on approvals. for the early benching we'd recommend Dedicated to get numbers, then replicate in Private before final signoff.
[00:05:58] Aisha Singh: okay, we'll start with Dedicated. pricing is a secondary discussion but important to assess perf per dollar.
[00:06:05] Maya Chen: we'll include cost-per-1M tokens estimates for each config in the followup.
[00:06:10] Sophia Reyes: on measurement, please be explicit about synthetic vs replay testing. we prefer replay from a 24-hour sample to capture real token distributions.
[00:06:18] Liam Patel: agreed — replay is best for representativeness. runbook will have both: replay harness and synthetic workloads for microbenching.
[00:06:25] Daniel Kim: for concurrency shaping, we'll need a harness that can model burst windows and diurnal patterns — can your script do that?
[00:06:32] Liam Patel: yes — the harness supports poisson/intermittent bursts and can replay timestamps from your logs. we'll include a yaml config for traffic shape.
[00:06:40] Sophia Reyes: excellent. what's your suggested acceptance criteria table we can use in the POC contract?
[00:06:47] Maya Chen: propose table: route name | workload (avg tokens out) | target TTFT_p95 | target TPOT_p95 | end-to-end p95 | end-to-end p99. For rerank: 40 tokens out, TTFT_p95 <=100ms, TPOT_p95 <=6ms/token, end-to-end p95 <=200ms, p99 <=500ms. For batch scoring route: 120 tokens out, TTFT less important, aim for TPOT_p95 <=10ms/token, throughput target X rps. we'll put concrete numbers in the doc.
[00:07:16] Aisha Singh: ok that's clear. please include measurement tolerances and test environment description. we need to know whether measurements include client network time; ideally we measure both client-observed and server-internal timings.
[00:07:29] Liam Patel: we do both — client-side RTT included and we also instrument server internal timing headers like X-Redwood-TTFT, X-Redwood-Decode-ms. runbook will show how to capture both.
[00:07:38] Sophia Reyes: how do you compute p99 for tails that are influenced by GC or noisy neighbors? we saw that on our infra.
[00:07:45] Liam Patel: we'll run multiple replicas and exclude cold-start windows, monitor GPU metrics and host-level noise, and correlate spikes with infra signals. for noisy neighbor mitigation we recommend dedicated pools. we'll also run a bootstrapped confidence interval over multiple runs to avoid overfitting to a single anomalous day.
[00:08:00] Daniel Kim: that sounds good. on instrumentation, what data will you share post-run?
[00:08:06] Maya Chen: deliverables: full raw latencies (per-request), aggregated p50/p90/p95/p99 tables, token-level decode traces for sample requests, GPU utilization charts, kernel/cuda metrics, and a short executive summary with pass/fail vs acceptance criteria.
[00:08:22] Sophia Reyes: great. any gotchas we should expect?
[00:08:26] Liam Patel: a few: tokenizer mode, batch padding inefficiencies, beam widths >1, and prefix caching effectiveness depend on prefix similarity. also watch out for sequence-length variance which affects TPOT non-linearly.
[00:08:40] Maya Chen: also note some transcriptions of our earlier trials had weird model name spellings in logs; don't worry about that, it's just the recorder.
[00:08:47] Sophia Reyes: (laughs) okay. security asks: we need SOC2 + ISO docs and audit log samples.
[00:08:53] Maya Chen: we'll include SOC2 and ISO attestation and sample audit logs in the followup packet.
[00:08:58] Aisha Singh: and SSO/SAML integration for the console?
[00:09:01] Maya Chen: yes, we support SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and RBAC for routes. we'll attach the security pack.
[00:09:07] Daniel Kim: one more technical: for TPOT measurement, do you separate tokenization/encoding time from decoding?
[00:09:12] Liam Patel: yes, the microbenchmarks separate tokenization (client-side), model encode+KV cache, and decode time per token; we'll report each component.
[00:09:20] Sophia Reyes: ok let's recap next steps.
[00:09:22] Maya Chen: recap: Redwood to send benchmark runbook, scripts, cost estimates, and SLO doc by Monday; Vectra to share sample dataset and traffic shapes by Wednesday; Redwood to run baseline Thursday; 7-day run Friday to Friday; follow-up results review next Tuesday.
[00:09:36] Sophia Reyes: confirmed.
[00:09:38] Aisha Singh: confirmed.
[00:09:40] Daniel Kim: confirmed.
[00:09:42] Liam Patel: i'll mute and start drafting the runbook now.
[00:09:45] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with attachments and calendar invites.
[00:09:50] Sophia Reyes: thanks much.
